title: Do We Need Asynchronous SGD? On the Near-Optimality of Synchronous Methods
claim: Synchronous-style rounds leave faster workers idle waiting for the slowest, so timing structure itself exposes the inefficiency.
layout: Single panel, 3 worker timelines left-to-right, vertical sync arrows to time axis
description: A schematic Gantt-style timeline with three horizontal rows labeled Worker 1, Worker 2 and Worker 3. Each row holds gray rounded boxes labeled τ_{i,j}, meaning the computation time of worker j in round i. Dashed empty boxes labeled 'bubble' follow the shorter tasks and show idle time. Worker 3 has the longest tasks, with no bubbles. Two thick vertical arrows drop from the end of each round to a time axis below. Dots on the axis are labeled x^1 and x^2, the synchronization points where the model is updated. A thin arrow labeled 'time' runs along the bottom. The figure is black and white with light gray fills. The eye goes first to the bubbles and the vertical sync lines.
caption: Wall-clock time visualization of Asynchronous SGD (Algorithm [ref]).
abstract: Modern distributed optimization methods mostly rely on traditional synchronous approaches, despite substantial recent progress in asynchronous optimization. We revisit Synchronous SGD and its robust variant, called $m$-Synchronous SGD, which can be interpreted as a method with a backup-worker strategy, and theoretically show that they are nearly optimal in many heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios, which is somewhat unexpected. We analyze the synchronous methods under random times and adversarial partial participation of workers, and prove that their time complexities are optimal in many practical regimes, up to logarithmic factors. While synchronous methods are not universal solutions and there exist tasks where asynchronous methods may be necessary, we show theoretically that they are sufficient for many modern heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios.
